Payroll would land at $208,135,388 if it were processed. The realistic paths are a third team absorbing the difference or getting the incoming salary renegotiated to $4,343,816 or below. There is no exception that covers an $820,591 shortfall for an apron team -- the 100% rule is absolute, and an $820,591 miss fails it exactly as decisively as a far larger one.

You are looking at $10,072,612 in luxury tax. Charlotte's tax salary is $177,308,064 against the $170,814,000 line, putting $6,494,064 into the tax, and as a standard rather than repeater payer you owe $1.50 per dollar on the first $5,168,000 for $7,752,000, then $1.75 per dollar on the remaining $1,326,064 for $2,320,612. Two things worth flagging beyond the total. You are only barely into the second bracket, so a modest salary reduction pulls you back into the $1.50 tier, and every marginal dollar currently costs $1.75 -- a favorable ratio compared with what deeper taxpayers face. The more consequential issue is repeater exposure: paying this season advances the clock, and repeater rates applied to this same $6,494,064 would be dramatically steeper. If ownership is tax-sensitive across a multi-year horizon, that overage is worth attacking now rather than next season. Also note that paying at all forfeits your share of the pool distributed to non-taxpaying teams.

**Verdict: LEGAL.** You are sending out more than you take back, which is what makes this work: $57,862,237 in Isaiah Okoro and Amari Halvorsen against $54,932,682 for Alperen Ferreira, under a 100% matching ceiling of $57,862,237. That is workable, but remember you are shedding two players for one, so the replacement signing comes out of that $11,821,414 rather than from anywhere else. And the honest assessment: at $196,002,586 you remain above the first apron afterward, so none of the tools you lost by crossing it come back. This saves money without changing your operating tier.

**Verdict: ILLEGAL.** The roster is full and the money does not fit -- you lose on both counts, and either one alone is dispositive. Brennan Achiuwa at $6,415,797 would push Washington from $191,250,888 to $197,666,685, which is $1,721,685 past your first apron hard cap of $195,945,000, and a hard cap is a genuine ceiling rather than a threshold with a penalty attached. Separately, you are carrying 15 players, so there is no spot to sign him into regardless of what the contract says. Before the signing you had $4,694,112 of room beneath $195,945,000, which is the relevant budget: a contract at or under that number clears the cap side, but you would still have to open a roster spot first. If Achiuwa is genuinely the target, waiving or trading a small contract solves both problems in one move -- it frees the spot and lowers the payroll, potentially far enough that the $6,415,797 fits.

At $215,009,900 Orlando is over the first apron of $209,015,000, and that crossing has already taken most of your signing tools off the shelf. The non-taxpayer mid-level and the bi-annual exception are both unavailable -- they disappear the moment you go over the first apron, and there is no mechanism to restore them mid-season. The room exception was never in play; it belongs to teams operating under the cap with actual room. What you have left is the taxpayer mid-level at $6,064,000 and minimum contracts. The taxpayer mid-level comes with a real string attached: spending any of it hard-caps you at the second apron of $221,686,000 for the rest of the league year, which would leave usable space from $215,009,900 but converts a threshold into a wall and forecloses absorbing salary at the deadline. Minimum deals are always available and trigger nothing, which with a full 15-man roster only matters once you open a spot. Practically, the taxpayer mid-level is your one real swing this season -- I would hold it until you know what the roster needs.
